paras: The killing of Israel Groff took place on November 7, 1882, election day, when Frederick, Maryland, policeman Porter shot Groff, a Black man, dead during a fight at a city polling precinct. A crowd that the National Republican put at several hundred Black men then surrounded the house of Judge John A. Lynch, where the officer had taken refuge, and threatened to lynch him before he was taken to jail. Porter was released on bail eleven days later, and accounts of why he fired differed sharply.

The 1882 congressional and judicial elections in Maryland were hard fought, and a Washington dispatch from Frederick that day reported "a great number of fights" in the county. According to the Shepherdstown Register, Porter was not keeping the peace at Precinct No. 1 but was "trying to buy colored voters for his party."

On the morning of the election a fight broke out at one of the Frederick precincts between a number of Black and white men. During it Porter shot Groff, who was about 28 years old, and killed him instantly; the Shepherdstown Register said two shots struck him in the chest.

Porter fled to the residence of Judge Lynch, a circuit court judge whom the Register identified as the Democratic candidate for associate judge. A crowd pursued him and gathered on the lawn demanding his surrender, while the sheriff and his deputies held him inside, and the Evening Star's correspondent reported that "threats are made of lynching the officer." Chief Judge Ritchie, Judge Lynch and others appealed for order, and the crowd eventually dispersed. In the meantime the sheriff took Porter to the jail by an indirect route; the Register said he was wrapped in blankets, carried over the back fence into a lumber yard and driven away in a wagon.

On November 18 Judge Lynch admitted Porter to bail, and a feared demonstration at the Court House did not occur. No report of an inquest, indictment or trial for the killing appears in the coverage. In late December Porter was charged with brutally assaulting a woman named Kate Hager; after citizens complained, the Board of Aldermen suspended him until January, and he resigned.

The Associated Press dispatch, headed in the Evening Star "A Colored Man Killed at the Polls in Frederick," was printed the same day and the next across the country, often shrunk to a single line in news summaries. Frederick County's Catoctin Clarion gave it one sentence, noting only that there "were but few election disturbances throughout the country."

Some papers went further: the Republican National Republican of Washington declared the shooting "nothing less than a deliberate murder," and the Shepherdstown Register headed its account "An Election Murder in Maryland." A syndicated crime column a week later took the opposite line, saying Groff had drawn a revolver and was shot before he could use it, and placed the event in Baltimore. Names were garbled in transmission, with the victim appearing as Graff, Isaac Gross and "John Israel Moore," and no Black newspaper account was found.

The Evening Star's Frederick correspondent reported "conflicting opinions" about the cause of the shooting. The Shepherdstown Register said Porter fired during a quarrel over a voter he was trying to buy, while the Martinsburg Independent reported the allegation that he shot at a man who had started the riot and refused arrest, hitting Groff by mistake. Only the later syndicated brief, which also misplaced the event, said Groff drew a weapon; the Frederick dispatches do not mention one.

reader.title: Killing of Israel Groff
bases: A Frederick policeman shot and killed a Black man at a polling precinct during an election-day fight (A1, A9, A12); the lynching talk concerned a crowd threatening the officer, not the victim (A2, A13).

The AP wire, a Washington special dispatch, the National Republican, a Frederick County weekly and West Virginia papers independently agree that Policeman Porter shot and killed Groff at a Frederick precinct on election day (A1, A2, A9, A12, A13, A14); only the cause is contested (A13, A14, A15).

accounts.label: AP wire
accounts.gist: During a fight between a number of negroes and whites at a Frederick precinct, Policeman Augustus Porter shot and instantly killed Israel Groff, colored.

accounts.label: Washington Republican paper
accounts.gist: Porter shot Groff in an altercation, fled to Judge Lynch's house, and was demanded by several hundred colored men; the paper called the killing 'a deliberate murder'.

accounts.label: Shepherdstown Register (anti-Porter partisan account)
accounts.gist: Porter, instead of keeping the peace, was buying colored voters for his party, quarreled over one, and fired two shots into Graff's chest; he was smuggled out in blankets to jail.

accounts.label: Martinsburg Independent ('it is alleged')
accounts.gist: The man who started the riot refused arrest; Porter drew his revolver and shot Groff, another party to the difficulty, by mistake.

accounts.label: Syndicated brief (officer's side)
accounts.gist: Groff drew a revolver on Policeman C. A. Porter and was shot before he could use it; places the event in Baltimore.

framing.detail: AP copy ran under heads such as 'A Colored Man Killed at the Polls in Frederick' and was reduced to one line in news summaries.
The National Republican said the shooting 'was nothing less than a deliberate murder'; the Shepherdstown Register headed its account 'An Election Murder in Maryland'.
The syndicated 'Crimes and Casualties' brief said Groff drew a revolver and was shot before he could use it.
The Evening Star's special dispatch noted 'conflicting opinions' on the cause and headlined the crowd's 'threats of lynching'.

record_check.dossier: No lynching of the victim; Groff was shot by a policeman. The only lynching threat was made by a crowd against the officer, who was not harmed.

record_check.record: Israel Graf, Israel Croft, Israel Groff, Israel Gron, Israel Golf, John Israel, Charles S. Porter
record_check.dossier: One victim, Israel Groff (Graff); the variants are spellings of his name, and Charles S. Porter is the policeman who shot him.
officers: a single policeman fired the shots.
Policeman Porter of Frederick (Augustus / Charles S. / C. A.).
Groff was not in custody; he was shot during a fight at the polls.

record_check.record: drew a revolver upon Policeman C. A. Porter
record_check.dossier: Only one syndicated brief says this; others say Porter was buying votes or shot Groff by mistake while making an arrest.
Frederick; Baltimore is an error in a condensed brief.
Killing by shooting; the siege and threat were directed by a crowd at the officer, not at the Black victim.

info: Election day, Tuesday, November 7, 1882, in the morning
A voting precinct in Frederick (Precinct No. 1 per the Shepherdstown Register); one syndicated brief wrongly places it in Baltimore
Israel Groff (also Graff, Graf, Gross, Grass, 'John Israel Moore'), colored, about 28 years old

Versions differ: the Batesville Guard brief says Groff drew a revolver on Porter; the Martinsburg Independent says Porter fired at a man who refused arrest and hit Groff by mistake; no accusation against Groff appears in the AP report
Policeman Porter of Frederick, given as Augustus, Charles S. or C. A. Porter
Porter admitted to bail by Judge Lynch on November 18; no report of an inquest, indictment or trial was found
